content: The bushel is a unit of measurement traditionally used in the United States customary system. It is primarily employed for measuring the volume of dry commodities, particularly in agricultural contexts, rather than liquids. The abbreviation for bushel is bsh. or bu. One bushel is equivalent to 36.872 liters or 8 Imperial gallons. However, in modern times, bushels are more commonly used as units of mass rather than volume. In the context of grain trading, whether on commodity markets or at local grain elevators, as well as in reports of grain production, bushels are defined as units of mass. This is achieved by assigning a standard weight to each commodity measured in bushels. For example, a bushel of wheat is standardized to weigh approximately 215 kilograms. Specific weight values are also defined for other commodities, such as different grains, oilseeds, fruits, vegetables, coal, and even hair. These definitions can vary depending on the jurisdiction, including differences between states within the United States. The United States government has adopted a policy to phase out traditional units like the bushel in favor of the metric system, which is used universally for scientific, technical, and most global purposes. As a result, understanding the relationship between the bushel and its metric equivalent, as well as whether it is being used as a unit of mass or volume, is essential. The term bushel has also been used historically to translate foreign units of similar size and origin, such as the German Scheffel. History The bushel was originally a measure of capacity for grain. During the Middle Ages, a bushel of wheat was expected to weigh 64 Tower pounds. However, when the Tower system was abolished in the 16th century, the bushel was redefined to weigh 56 avoirdupois pounds. The bushel was rarely used in Scotland, Ireland, or Wales during the Middle Ages. Before and during the 19th century, there were even more variations of gallon measurements in use.
